You express concession and contrast (benché, sebbene, nonostante + congiuntivo, anche se, malgrado, pur + gerund, eppure, comunque) to say that something happens despite an obstacle.
the piggy bank, the money box
Although the restoration is half done, we have to stop.
Even if it's hard, we won't give up.
Despite the cold, they worked all day.
Although I understand your anger, I can't do anything.
Sixty thousand euros were missing. And yet they found them.
To use benché, sebbene, nonostante + congiuntivo: Benché sia tardi, resto.
To use anche se + indicative: Anche se è tardi, resto.
To use malgrado / nonostante + noun: malgrado il freddo.
To use pur + gerund: Pur essendo stanca, lavora.
To link opposing ideas with eppure, tuttavia, però, comunque.
To use per quanto, qualunque, chiunque, dovunque + congiuntivo.
Syracuse, mid-January. Bellini and Giulia are called into the office of the superintendent of the Heritage Authority, Dr Russo.
I'm sorry, but although the restoration is half done, we have to stop. The donor has withdrawn the funding.
What? Despite all the work we've done?
Even if I wanted to, I couldn't do anything. The company that was funding us went bankrupt last week.
However difficult the situation may be, Dr Russo, you don't leave a Caravaggio half done.
Professor, although I understand your anger, without money I can't pay for the materials or the scaffolding.
We can work for free for a few weeks. Although we have a little girl, we'll manage.
Despite your generosity, we're still sixty thousand euros short.
Sixty thousand. Fine. We'll find it.
And where, may I ask? Any bank would say no to you.
I don't know yet. And yet we'll find it. I have seventy years of stubbornness in my family.
I may have an idea. Even if it sounds strange. Ortigia loves its Totò.
Madam, anyone who wants to help is welcome. You have a month. After that, we take down the scaffolding.
ben-KAY, with a closed "e" at the end. seb-BE-ne, double BB.
Stress on "DAJ": te-star-DAJ-jee-ne. GG + I = a long "j".
The conjunctions "benché", "sebbene", "nonostante (che)" and "malgrado (che)" mean "although" and take the SUBJUNCTIVE:
Benché il restauro sia a metà, dobbiamo fermarci.
Sebbene abbiamo una bambina, ce la faremo.
Although we have a little girl, we'll manage.
Although it was raining, they went out.
Benché avesse settant’anni, lavorava ogni giorno.
Although he was seventy, he worked every day.
In English (and Romanian) "although" is followed by the indicative ("although it is late"). In Italian: "benché SIA tardi", NOT "benché è tardi". Remember: it's the same as in chapter 26.
"Anche se" (even if, although) is the most common in speech and takes the INDICATIVE. With the congiuntivo imperfetto it becomes hypothetical:
Anche se è difficile, non ci arrendiamo.
If you're not sure which to choose, "anche se + indicative" is always correct and natural.
Pur capendo la sua rabbia, non posso fare niente.
"Pur + gerund" is used when the subject is the SAME in both parts. It's very elegant in writing.
These adverbs link two independent clauses that contrast:
Mancavano sessantamila euro. Eppure li hanno trovati.
Il progetto è costoso; tuttavia è necessario.
Non so come, comunque li troveremo.
5. Per quanto, qualunque, chiunque, dovunque + congiuntivo
Words meaning "however much", "whatever / any", "whoever", "wherever" also take the subjunctive:
However difficult the situation may be, we won't stop.
Anyone who wants to help is welcome.
Whatever happens, we'll finish the restoration.
Wherever you go, I'll follow you.
"Qualunque" goes before a SINGULAR noun and doesn't change: "qualunque cosa", "qualunque banca", NOT "qualunque banche".
Il donatore ha ritirato i fondi
Che cosa è successo alla ditta?
Di lavorare gratis per qualche settimana

Giulia's idea was simple, even though nobody believed in it. Although sixty thousand euros was an enormous sum for a small town, Ortigia had something the banks didn't have: it had Totò. Ever since Pietro had given him a name, the child hidden in the Caravaggio had become a sort of mascot for the neighbourhood. People talked about him in the bars, children drew him, and one pastry cook had even invented a cake, "the Totò", with pistachio.

So, on the first of February, next to the panel with the X-ray, an old terracotta money box shaped like a fish appeared. Above it, Turi had written in his shaky handwriting: "One euro for Totò. Help us finish the restoration." On the first day thirty-two euros and a button went into it. "Few as they are," Turi said, counting them on the altar, "they're a start."

Then word got around. Concetta began selling her lemons in front of the church, one euro each, and although she was eighty, she stood there from eight until one, with the sea wind tousling her white hair. In two weeks she sold one thousand two hundred lemons. "Whatever happens," she told her customers, "this lemon will bring you luck. It comes from the tree I was married under."

The fishermen in the harbour, although the winter had been poor for fish, organised a dinner on the quay: grilled swordfish for three hundred people, ten euros a head. Half the neighbourhood came, and even though it was raining, nobody left before midnight. At the end the head of the fishermen, an enormous man called Saro, handed Giulia an envelope with four thousand euros and said: "For the boy. We've all been out at sea in the dark. We know what it means."

The news reached Naples, where Grandma Assunta, although she hardly ever left the house any more, persuaded all the women in her neighbourhood to give ten euros each. There were forty-two of them. In Florence, Graziella put a money box on the trattoria counter, with a photo of Viola and the words "For Viola's little brother", even though Totò, strictly speaking, was nobody's brother.

Money even arrived from Sibiu. Ion had told the story to his old railway colleagues, who, although they had never seen a Caravaggio in their lives, had taken up a collection. Along with the money, in an envelope, was a photograph of forty retired railwaymen in front of an old locomotive, holding a sign written in touching Italian: "Forza Totò! Da Romania con amore."

Pietro, in Florence, wanted to do his bit too. Although he was only ten, he persuaded his teacher to organise a cake sale at his school. Graziella made twenty tarts, Signor Franco was the cashier with an old wooden box, and Marco and Sara bought half the cakes themselves. In the end Pietro raised three hundred and twenty euros. He sent them to Syracuse with a letter: "Dear Totò, even though we've never met, I'm the one who gave you your name. So you're a bit like my brother."

The schools of Syracuse put on an exhibition of drawings. There were hundreds of Totòs: Totò playing football, Totò eating granita, Totò climbing out of the painting and going to the beach. A six-year-old had drawn Totò sleeping under a black blanket, with a speech bubble saying: "Let me sleep, but finish the painting." Bellini bought that drawing for a hundred euros and hung it above his desk.

Meanwhile Matei and Giulia kept working on the scaffolding, for free, despite the cold in the church and the sleepless nights. Viola stayed with Turi, or with Concetta, or with whoever was free that morning. By now half of Ortigia knew how to change a nappy. "Although I've never had children," Turi would say, "now I have a granddaughter. And a granddaughter who already knows how to clap when the organ plays."

On the twenty-eighth of February, the last day of the month Dr Russo had granted, Turi opened the fish-shaped money box on the altar in front of everyone. Giulia counted three times, her hands shaking. Lemons, the fishermen's dinner, Assunta's neighbours, Graziella's trattoria, the railwaymen of Sibiu, the schools, the money box: fifty-eight thousand euros. Two thousand were still missing. However hard they had tried, two thousand euros were missing.

There was a long silence in the church. Then Turi bent down to pick up something that had fallen out of the money box along with the coins: a white envelope, sealed, with no name. Inside were twenty hundred-euro notes and a handwritten note, in elegant handwriting that Matei and Giulia would have recognised among a thousand: "For Totò. From an old gentleman who used to restore paintings."

Everyone turned towards Bellini, who was standing at the back of the church with his hands behind his back. "Don't look at me," he said. "I'm still in service until September. I can't be 'an old gentleman who used to restore'." And yet, as he said it, he was smiling as nobody had ever seen him smile. Giulia ran to him and hugged him, even though he was the least huggable man in the whole of Italy.

The next day Dr Russo signed the documents. The restoration would continue to the end. And on the fish-shaped money box, which Turi never wanted to take away again, someone added a little sign: "Thank you, Ortigia. Totò."
